summary: A 1980 specification of the DoD standard Transmission Control Protocol, an early form of TCP for reliable data streams. It was replaced by RFC 793 and RFC 7805, and it is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 761 specifies TCP as a reliable connection between processes on different hosts. It uses sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmission, and flow control to deliver data in order, and it has since been replaced by newer RFCs.

questions: how does tcp deliver data reliably
subtitle: A 1980 specification for reliable, ordered communication between processes.

tldr.problem: Applications need reliable communication even when the underlying network can lose, duplicate, damage, delay, or reorder data.
tldr.mechanism: TCP numbers each data octet, acknowledges received data, retransmits after a timeout, checks a checksum, and controls sending with a receiver-advertised window.
tldr.outcome: RFC 761 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 793 and RFC 7805.

facts.label: Named control bits
facts.value: URG, ACK, EOL, RST, SYN, FIN

sections.title: TCP's Role Between Applications and IP
sections.content:
The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) provides reliable communication between processes on hosts in interconnected networks. It runs above the Internet Protocol (IP), which provides a potentially unreliable datagram service, and below higher-level protocols such as Telnet and file transfer.

TCP presents a connection-oriented service. Applications can open and close connections and send and receive data; TCP handles delivery across the underlying network.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP connects application processes on different computers. It works above IP and manages reliable data delivery for the applications using it.

sections.title: Reliable Delivery and Flow Control
sections.content:
TCP assigns a sequence number to every data octet. The receiver acknowledges the next octet it expects, so an acknowledgment also covers earlier octets. The sender keeps transmitted data until it is acknowledged and retransmits it if its timer expires. The receiver uses sequence numbers to reorder data and remove duplicates; a checksum lets it detect and discard damaged segments.

The receiver advertises a window of sequence numbers it is prepared to accept. TCP can carry a continuous stream of octets or records called letters; an end-of-letter marker tells TCP to forward that record promptly.
sections.plainLanguage: Sequence numbers let the receiver put data in order and spot duplicates. Acknowledgments trigger retransmission when needed, while a window tells the sender how much the receiver can accept.

sections.title: The TCP Segment Header
sections.content:
The TCP header identifies source and destination ports, carries sequence and acknowledgment numbers, and records a data offset, reserved bits, control bits, a window, a checksum, and an urgent pointer. The source and destination port fields are each 16 bits; sequence and acknowledgment numbers are each 32 bits.

The named control bits are URG, ACK, EOL, RST, SYN, and FIN. Options may follow the fixed fields, and zero padding aligns the end of the header to a 32-bit boundary. The checksum covers the header and data plus a pseudo header containing source and destination addresses, protocol, and TCP length.
sections.plainLanguage: The header identifies the ports, numbers the data, and carries control and error-checking information. Its flags help TCP acknowledge data, open or close connections, and signal urgent data.

sections.title: Opening and Closing a Connection
sections.content:
A connection is identified by the pair of sockets at its ends. Each socket combines an internet address with a port. The two TCPs synchronize their initial sequence numbers with a three-way handshake: one sends SYN, the other responds with SYN and an acknowledgment, and the first acknowledges the reply.

The handshake helps prevent delayed or duplicate connection requests from being mistaken for a new connection. To close, each side signals that it has no more data to send with FIN; the other side acknowledges it and can continue receiving until it also closes.

RFC 761 also uses IP's type-of-service field and security option to provide precedence and security on a per-connection basis. Implementations in multilevel security environments should mark outgoing segments and let users request those values.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers exchange three messages to synchronize sequence numbers before treating a connection as established. Each side can close its sending direction while still receiving data from the other, and the specification carries precedence and security information through IP.
